title: Structured Hamiltonian Learning for Multiqubit Conditional Phase Gates
abstract: Accurate measurement of an intended conditional phase does not by itself place a multiqubit phase gate in its declared generalized-gate equivalence class. We cast the diagnosis as structured Hamiltonian learning of the diagonal successful block in a known basis: Ramsey measurements on a connected graph reconstruct a target-relative eigenphase map; a Walsh transform then yields the per-cycle stroboscopic error generator in a selected logarithm branch, whose branch-dependent coefficients alone cannot decide global equivalence. For diagonal Pauli-Z dressing of weight at most m we derive an exact branch-independent criterion from multiplicative Boolean-Mobius invariants, converted at finite shot counts into a pass/fail/unresolved decision under prespecified tolerances and simultaneous confidence, separate from model rejection. For shared-control C^mZ gates a circular target-face contrast isolates each intended conditional phase, yet a support theorem exhibits forbidden interactions invisible to every target face once multiple targets or external spectators are present. We derive a Cramer-Rao bound for arbitrary integer phase contrasts, recovering the 4^m attempted-circuit scaling of a uniform (m+1)-body face, and quantify degradation from visibility loss, heralded survival, readout confusion, and correlated noise, while systematic bias triggers model rejection. Seeded simulations implement the 4M-setting multiplexed acquisition end to end: for M=3,4,5 at a common budget its mean phase-map RMSE is 0.689-0.794 times a separately compiled statewise scan, and a blind-interaction test yields 300/300 global-audit rejections versus 1/300 for target faces. These results estimate the error generator of a diagonal successful block under a specified acquisition model; they are not unknown-basis Hamiltonian identification, arbitrary-channel tomography, or hardware certification.
summary: This paper develops a sophisticated theoretical framework to certify the global equivalence class of multiqubit conditional phase gates, addressing the limitation that local measurements are insufficient for this task. It introduces multiplicative Boolean-Möbius invariants as a branch-independent criterion for global membership. The work is highly relevant for quantum computing hardware certification by providing a robust diagnostic tool.
main_problem: The core problem is determining if a measured multiqubit conditional phase gate belongs to its declared generalized-gate equivalence class, distinguishing global equivalence from local measurement outcomes.
main_result: The authors derived an exact, branch-independent criterion for global equivalence using multiplicative Boolean-Möbius invariants, and demonstrated that local measurements are insufficient to guarantee global membership.
method: The methodology combines Ramsey measurements to reconstruct a target-relative eigenphase map, followed by applying a Walsh transform to yield the error generator, and finally using Möbius invariants for a global class membership test.
model_or_system: The system involves multiqubit conditional phase gates, modeled by a structured Hamiltonian representing a diagonal successful block in a known basis. The analysis focuses on the error generator $	ext{Herr}$ and its relationship to the target-relative unitary $U_{	ext{err}}$.
key_observables: Multiplicative Boolean-Möbius invariants ($	ext{M}_T[u]$), the relative phase $\epsilon(z)$, and the mean phase-map RMSE from multiplexed acquisition.
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($m$), the number of multiplexing settings ($M=3, 4, 5$), and specified tolerances/confidence levels for statistical decision-making.
main_assumptions: The results estimate the error generator under a specified acquisition model, and the method explicitly separates global equivalence-class membership from the local error generator estimation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the structured Hamiltonian learning process, showing how global invariants fix the allowed group, Ramsey counts yield local phases via a Walsh chart, and target faces can miss forbidden interactions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the global equivalence problem (Möbius invariants) to local estimation (Ramsey/Walsh transforms) and culminates in rigorous statistical bounds (Cramér-Rao) and a multi-step experimental protocol for deployment.
why_interesting: This work provides a mathematically rigorous framework for certifying the global equivalence class of quantum gates, moving beyond simple local fidelity checks which are known to be insufficient.
